title: Maximum Xor
directAnswer: For each query x, find the array element that maximizes x ^ element. Brute force tests x against every element: O(n) per query, O(n·q) total. The optimal answer inserts all numbers into a binary trie (one node per bit, most-significant first) and, for each query, walks the trie greedily taking the OPPOSITE bit at every level when it exists — that sets the highest possible bits of the XOR. Build is O(n·B); each query is O(B) where B is the bit width.

remember.pattern: Greedy high-bit choice over a binary (bitwise) trie
remember.formula:
build: insert every num bit-by-bit, MSB → LSB
query(x):
    res = 0
    for bit from B down to 0:
        want = 1 - ((x >> bit) & 1)   # opposite bit maximizes XOR
        if child[want] exists: res |= (1 << bit); go to child[want]
        else:                  go to child[1 - want]
    return res
rules: **XOR of two bits is 1 only when they differ.** To maximize x ^ y, you want y's bit to be the OPPOSITE of x's bit at every position.
Process bits **most-significant first** — a single high bit outweighs all lower bits combined, so the greedy choice is locally and globally optimal.
Only set `res |= (1 << bit)` when the opposite branch actually exists; otherwise you must follow the same-bit branch and that position contributes 0.
Fix the bit width `B` from the constraints (values ≤ 10⁹ → 30 bits is enough; use 30 or 31). Looping too few bits drops the high bits of the answer.
Brute force first (O(n) per query) to show the progression, then introduce the trie as the way to answer each query in O(B).
whenToUse: Repeated 'maximum/minimum XOR of x against a set' queries
You can preprocess the set once and answer many queries fast
Max-XOR-pair problems (insert as you scan, query against what's seen)
Anything where a per-bit greedy decision composes the optimum
antiSignals: A single query over a single array → just one linear scan, no trie
You need the XOR subset/total, not a max against a target → think prefix-XOR or parity
Range/index constraints on the partner (l ≤ a ≤ b ≤ r) → that's Maximizing XOR, a closed-form, not a trie
Memory is tight and B·n nodes won't fit → consider sorting-based or offline tricks
remember.takeaway: Max-XOR against a set is the canonical bit-trie problem: store numbers by their bits, then greedily chase the opposite bit from the top down. The same trie powers Maximum XOR of Two Numbers and Maximum XOR With an Element From Array — learn it once, reuse everywhere.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you see that maximizing XOR is a per-bit greedy decision (take the opposite bit, high to low) and can back it with a binary trie so each query is O(B) instead of O(n).
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Doing the O(n) scan per query and stopping there, or building the trie but going to the SAME bit instead of the opposite, or processing bits least-significant first so the greedy choice is no longer optimal.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the brute force and its O(n·q) cost, then explain why opposite-bit-from-the-top is optimal (a high bit dominates), and note the trie answers each query in O(B) after an O(n·B) build.

problemStatement: You are given an array `arr` of non-negative integers and a list of queries. For each query value `x`, find the maximum value of `x XOR arr[i]` over all elements `arr[i]` in the array, and return these maxima in order.
constraints: Each query is answered independently against the full array
understanding: We are not maximizing a sum but an XOR. XOR sets a result bit to 1 exactly when the two input bits differ, so the best partner for a query x is the number whose bits disagree with x in the highest positions. Because the array is fixed and many queries arrive, it pays to preprocess the numbers into a structure that makes 'find the most opposite number, bit by bit' fast — a binary trie.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the numbers non-negative and bounded?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — non-negative and ≤ 10⁹, so 30 bits is enough. I'll use a fixed bit width (30 or 31) for every number, including its leading zeros.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many queries are there relative to n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 10⁵ queries against up to 10⁵ elements. That's why a per-query O(n) scan (10¹⁰ ops) is too slow and the trie's O(B) query matters.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array change between queries?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — it's fixed. So I build the trie once and reuse it for all queries. If it changed, I'd insert/remove nodes per update.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I return values or indices?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Values of the maximum XOR, not indices. The trie naturally yields the best XOR value; recovering the index would need extra bookkeeping.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Decision tree. Maximum Xor is the many-queries-against-a-fixed-set branch — preprocess into a bit trie.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Scan Every Element Per Query
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to frame the cost. It's the literal reading of the problem and sets up why the trie is needed.
hints: For a single query x, how would you find the best partner? Just try them all and keep the largest XOR.
Loop over every element, compute x ^ element, track the maximum.
Now repeat that scan for each of the q queries. That's n·q work — fine for tiny inputs, too slow at 10⁵ × 10⁵.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each query scans all n elements doing O(1) XOR work; q queries give n·q ≈ 10¹⁰ in the worst case — far beyond a one-second budget.
approaches.explanation:
Translate the question directly: for each query value `x`, walk the entire array, compute `x ^ arr[i]` for every element, and keep the largest.

**Why it's the natural first attempt.** The problem literally asks for the maximum of `x ^ arr[i]` over all `i`. A linear scan that evaluates exactly that expression for every element is correct by construction — no insight required.

**Why it doesn't scale.** A single scan is `O(n)`, which is great for one query. But with up to `10⁵` queries against up to `10⁵` elements, the total is `n·q ≈ 10¹⁰` XOR operations. That blows the time limit. The fix is to stop re-scanning the whole array for every query and instead preprocess the numbers so each query only inspects `B` bits.

**The bridge to the trie.** Notice that for a fixed `x`, the best partner is decided bit by bit: at the highest bit we'd love an element whose bit is the opposite of `x`'s. The brute force rediscovers that ranking from scratch every time; a trie bakes the bit structure in once.
approaches.insight: Maximizing an XOR is a most-significant-bit-first decision: the partner you want disagrees with x as high up as possible. Brute force re-derives that for every query — the trie remembers it.

dryRun.intro: Compute x ^ element for every element and keep the running maximum.

code.python:
def maxXor(arr: list[int], queries: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    result = []
    for x in queries:
        best = 0
        for a in arr:                      # try every partner
            best = max(best, x ^ a)
        result.append(best)
    return result

java.explanation: Evaluate the exact quantity to maximize for this element and keep the largest seen.
Store the per-query answer; the array is never modified between queries.

python.explanation: Compute x ^ a for each element and track the maximum.
Record this query's answer before moving to the next query.

pitfalls: Initializing best to a wrong sentinel — start at 0 (XOR is non-negative) or at the first computed XOR.
Re-scanning the array per query when q and n are both large — this is the O(n·q) trap.
Returning an index instead of the maximum XOR value.

approaches.name: Binary Trie — Greedy Opposite-Bit Walk (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'store the numbers in a bit trie, then for each query take the opposite bit from the top down'.
hints: XOR's bit is 1 only when the two bits differ. So to maximize x ^ y, at each bit you want y's bit to be the opposite of x's.
Store every number in a binary trie: depth = bit position, two children (0 and 1), inserted most-significant bit first.
To query x, descend from the root: at each level try the child equal to the OPPOSITE of x's bit (set that result bit); if it's missing, follow the only child available. B levels → O(B) per query.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Inserting n numbers touches B nodes each → O(n·B). Each of the q queries descends B levels → O(q·B). Space is the trie: at most n·B nodes. With B ≈ 30 this is effectively linear.
approaches.explanation:
Preprocess the array into a binary trie, then answer each query by greedily chasing the opposite bit.

**Why opposite-bit-from-the-top is optimal.** XOR yields a 1 in a position exactly when the two operands differ there. A 1 in a higher position is worth more than all lower positions combined (`2^k > 2^k − 1 = sum of all lower bits`). So to maximize `x ^ y`, the single most valuable thing is to make the highest bit of the result a 1 — which means picking a `y` whose top bit differs from `x`'s. Lock that in, then recurse on the next bit with the same logic. This greedy choice never needs revisiting because no combination of lower bits can ever beat one higher bit.

**Why a trie.** We need to ask, at each level, 'does the set contain a number that, so far, matches the prefix I've committed to AND has the opposite bit next?' A trie keyed by bits answers exactly that in O(1) per level: the children of the current node ARE the numbers consistent with the prefix walked so far. Following the opposite child when it exists keeps us on the best possible partner; when it's absent we're forced to the same bit and that position contributes 0.

**Why most-significant first.** Insertion and query must agree on bit order, and the greedy argument only holds top-down. Inserting and querying from the MSB means the first decision is the most significant bit, exactly where the greedy payoff is largest.

**Width discipline.** Use a fixed `B` (30 covers 10⁹; 31 is safe). Loop `i` from `B` down to `0` for both insert and query so leading zeros are represented consistently.
approaches.insight: A bitwise trie turns 'find the most opposite number' into a single root-to-leaf walk: at every level greedily branch away from the query's bit. The whole optimization is recognizing that maximizing XOR is a high-bit-first greedy decision, and a trie is the structure that makes each greedy step O(1).

java.explanation: Insert/query most-significant bit first so the greedy choice attacks the highest-value bit first.
XOR is 1 when bits differ — the opposite of x's bit is what maximizes this position.
Only take the opposite branch if some number actually has that prefix; otherwise we're forced the other way.
We secured a differing bit at position i, so this bit of the XOR is 1.

python.explanation: Walk bits high to low for both insert and query so they stay consistent.
The partner bit that differs from x's bit makes this XOR bit a 1.
Take the opposite branch when it exists; that keeps us on the best possible partner.
Record the 1 bit we just earned in the result.

edgeCases.behavior: Only one path exists; the walk is forced to 8 and returns 1 ^ 8 = 9.
Every element equals x; no opposite bit is ever available, so the walk yields 5 ^ 5 = 0.

pitfalls: Going to the SAME bit instead of the opposite — that minimizes XOR rather than maximizing it.
Processing bits least-significant first — the greedy choice is only optimal top-down.
Using too few bits for B and silently dropping the high bits of large numbers.
Forgetting to fall back to child[b] when child[want] is null — leads to a null-pointer walk.

commonMistakes: Answering each query with an O(n) scan and never building the trie — too slow when n and q are both large.
Descending to the same bit as the query instead of the opposite bit, which minimizes the XOR.
Choosing a bit width that's too small, dropping the most significant bits of the answer.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Greedy toward the same bit
commonMistakesDetailed.why: XOR is 1 only when bits differ. Taking the child equal to x's bit makes the XOR bit 0 and minimizes the result.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int b = (x >> i) & 1;
if (node.child[b] != null) node = node.child[b];   // same bit → minimizes
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
int want = 1 - ((x >> i) & 1);
if (node.child[want] != null) { res |= (1 << i); node = node.child[want]; }

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Bits processed low-to-high
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The greedy 'take the opposite bit' is only globally optimal from the most significant bit down; reversing the order can pick a worse high bit.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for i in range(0, B + 1):        # LSB first — greedy no longer optimal
    ...
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for i in range(B, -1, -1):       # MSB first
    ...

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Width too small
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If B is smaller than the number of significant bits, the top bits never enter the trie and the maximum XOR is undercounted.

followupVariations.title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array
followupVariations.hint: Insert each number then query it against the trie of the rest — same greedy walk, no separate query list.

followupVariations.title: Maximum XOR With an Element From Array
followupVariations.hint: Add an upper-bound constraint (element ≤ m). Sort queries and insert numbers up to m offline, then query the trie.

followupVariations.title: Maximizing XOR
followupVariations.hint: When the partner is constrained to a range l..r, the answer is a closed form from the leading differing bit — no trie needed.

patternNote: Bitwise trie + high-bit-first greedy. Whenever you must maximize (or minimize) an XOR of a value against a set, store the set by bits and walk toward the opposite (or same) bit from the MSB down. This is the backbone of Maximum XOR of Two Numbers and its constrained variants.
